headline: US-Iran truce lapses, Trump threatens Oman, another ship hit exiting Hormuz - crude finally responds
client_frame_short:
You will hear that we threatened to bomb Oman overnight and that another ship was hit leaving the Persian Gulf, and your first thought will be the four dollars a gallon you paid this weekend. That cost is real — about a dollar a gallon more than last summer. But a higher gas bill and a threat to your retirement are two different conversations, and you only have the first one.

Here is what the coverage will miss. Oil is up about three percent in two days and stocks barely moved — the S&P closed half a percent lower and sits less than one percent below last week's record. **That gap is the market pricing a shipping problem, not a shutdown.** There is nothing for you to do today. What I am watching is tomorrow afternoon's Fed minutes, because what could actually hurt a balanced portfolio here is rates staying high, not the tankers.
client_frame:
The setup flipped overnight, and the flip is the story. Yesterday the striking fact was that Hormuz traffic had gone to zero over the weekend and crude fell anyway. Since then the escalation changed character: the 60-day US-Iran understanding lapsed Monday with no deal (Al Jazeera), President Trump threatened to bomb Oman — the country mediating the transit talks — in a Fox News interview (Wall Street Journal), and at 11:32 PM ET a vessel outbound through the strait was struck by a projectile, damaging its engine room and killing a crew member (UKMTO via Al Jazeera). Crude stopped shrugging. Brent settled at $90.87 and WTI at $84.50, both up roughly 2.6% on the day.

The equity reaction stayed orderly, and that matters. The S&P fell half a percent Monday, the VIX is still under 16, and Nasdaq futures are down about 1% this morning. That is a market pricing a persistent shipping tax on oil, not a closed strait. Hormuz transits did recover slightly, to 6 vessels Monday against a 10-day average of 11 (Reuters, citing Kpler) — constrained, but flowing.

The real transmission channel is not equities, it is rates. The 30-year Treasury yield is hovering near its highest level since 2002 (CNBC), Japan's 10-year hit 2.94%, a level unseen since 1996 (Reuters), and odds of a Fed hike in September rose to 36% from 33% on Friday (CME). Gold is the confirming tell: it gained 1.27% Monday to $4,425 while yields rose, which is a geopolitical and inflation hedge bid, not a bet on falling rates. Higher oil feeds inflation, inflation keeps the Fed tight, and a tight Fed repricing the long end is what actually pressures a 60/40 portfolio.

Home Depot gave the cleanest read on the domestic economy. It beat on both lines and comps rose 1.7%, but management only reaffirmed guidance rather than raising it, and the CFO described operating in "frozen housing market conditions" (CNBC). Housing is where high rates bite first.

For clients: separate the household cost of gasoline from the portfolio question, because they are not the same conversation. The portfolio risk in this story runs through interest rates and inflation, not through the Strait of Hormuz itself. Tomorrow's FOMC minutes at 2:00 PM and the Canada tariff deadline at 12:01 AM are the two dated catalysts this week; the war headlines are not, on their own, a reason to change an allocation.
geo_headlines: THE FLIP: yesterday Hormuz transits hit zero and crude fell anyway. Overnight the escalation changed character and crude responded - Brent settled $90.87, WTI $84.50, both about +2.6% Monday. Brent is flat this morning at $90.82; WTI is up to ~$85.00.

The 60-day US-Iran understanding signed in Islamabad lapsed Monday with no deal. Iran's foreign ministry called the deadline provision "moot," saying the US had already violated the memorandum (Al Jazeera).

Trump told Fox News "if Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s--- out of them," referring to Oman's role mediating Hormuz transit talks, and called on Iran to raise "the white flag of surrender" (Wall Street Journal, New York Times). Iran said separately that talks with Oman on a transit-route map are "continuing in earnest."

UKMTO warning 115-26: a vessel outbound through the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile at 03:32 UTC (11:32 PM ET Monday), damaging the engine room and causing one crew fatality. Omani Coast Guard assisting (Al Jazeera, UKMTO).

Hormuz transits recovered only slightly - 6 vessels Monday (3 in, 3 out) against a 10-day average of 11, after 0 on Sunday and 5 on Saturday (Reuters, citing Kpler). Constrained but flowing, not closed.

Bessent's promised "unprecedented" Iran measures STILL not announced. A direct check of OFAC's own recent-actions page shows nothing after Aug 12, and the most recent Iran-specific action remains Aug 7. This is a live, undated catalyst - not a calendar event.

CORRECTION CARRIED FORWARD: there is no August 21 Iran sanctions cliff. OFAC revoked General License X on July 7 and the successor license's wind-down ended July 17. Stale June-dated law-firm alerts still circulate the Aug 21 date.

RATES ARE THE REAL STORY: US 30Y near its highest since 2002 (CNBC), Japan's 10Y JGB at 2.94%, a 30-year high, on September BoJ hike bets and weak Q2 GDP (Reuters). Gold +1.27% Monday to $4,425 WHILE yields rose - a hedge bid, not a duration trade.

Canada: still no deal with roughly 17 hours to go. LeBlanc and Charette met Greer and Lutnick in Washington Monday; officials said the sides were "not close" (iPolitics). Carney called talks "delicate" and "intense" and said he expects to speak with Trump within 48 hours (CBC). 50% on ~$20.2B of goods, no USMCA exemption, 12:01 AM Wednesday.

Home Depot beat: adj EPS $4.92 vs ~$4.72 consensus, revenue $47.9B vs ~$47.2B, comps +1.7% vs +0.9% expected - but guidance only REAFFIRMED, and CFO McPhail described "frozen housing market conditions" (CNBC, Reuters). CEO Ted Decker remains on medical leave and did not join the call.

Monday's data ran hot: Empire State manufacturing jumped to 20.6, its highest in more than four years, versus ~10-11 expected and 15.6 prior (New York Fed). NAHB builder confidence 35 vs 33 expected (NAHB).
Fed hike odds rose on the fresh Monday cohort: September now 36.07% for +25bp versus 33.07% on Friday's cohort; December carries a 20.1% chance of +50 or more (CME direct).

AAA national gasoline average $4.065, up about a dollar a year over year (AAA). Guardian, citing AAA, reports this is the highest ever recorded for August - a superlative we could not re-verify against AAA's own historical series.

Houthi forces claimed a missile strike on a Saudi military landing ship near Mokha in the Red Sea; RFE/RL reports six killed on a related cargo vessel south of Mokha. Saudi officials had not confirmed as of publication.

Deals: Nvidia guaranteeing up to $105B of OpenAI's Ohio data-center lease (WSJ; note WSJ separately headlines a downsizing from an original $250B plan - unreconciled). Raytheon won a $22.9B, seven-year Navy Tomahawk contract. AvalonBay/Equity Residential closed as Vivmark Residential (VMRK), ~$70B EV, trading today.

DISCLOSED GAP: Asian index closes showed unusually wide dispersion across sources this morning (KOSPI prints ranged from -1.55% to +0.66%), so no Asia levels are shown above. The region was broadly lower on oil and geopolitical risk; KOSPI did reopen after Monday's holiday. Confirm on a terminal before trading off Asia numbers.
